items.prompt: Why does a whale breathe through a blowhole on top of its head instead of through a nose and mouth like a land mammal?

options.label: The nostrils shifted to the top of the skull over generations
options.feedback: Positioned there and sealed by a muscular flap, the blowhole lets a whale take a breath the instant just a sliver of its head breaks the surface.

options.label: A whale's mouth is too full of teeth to breathe through
options.feedback: Land mammals breathe through the mouth as well as the nose despite having teeth. Tooth count is not the reason breathing moved elsewhere.

options.label: Water pressure forced the nostrils upward over a whale's lifetime
options.feedback: Pressure acting on one individual during its life could not reshape where its nostrils sit. This is a change built into the species over many generations.

options.label: The blowhole is a completely new organ with no equivalent in land mammals
options.feedback: It is the same nostril every land mammal has, just relocated. Nothing new was invented; something familiar simply moved.

items.ok_line: The same nostril every mammal has, just moved to the top of the head.
items.ko_line: Think about what a whale needs to expose above water to take a breath, and how little of its body that requires.
items.exp_title: A nostril moved to the top
items.exp_text: Over many generations, the nostril openings of whale ancestors gradually shifted backward along the skull until they sat on top of the head rather than at the front of the face. A ring of muscle keeps the blowhole sealed shut by default, opening only for the brief moment a whale rises to breathe, so barely any of its body needs to break the surface to take a full breath before diving again. That placement lets a whale breathe with barely a ripple, even while swimming at speed just beneath the surface.

items.prompt: How does a thick layer of blubber keep a whale warm in cold ocean water?

options.label: Fat conducts heat away from the body far more slowly than muscle does
options.feedback: Wrapped just beneath the skin, that slow-conducting layer keeps the warmth generated deep inside the body from escaping into water that would otherwise drain it away fast.

options.label: It traps a layer of air the way fur does
options.feedback: Blubber is solid fat, with no air held inside it. It insulates through the fat itself, not through any trapped air.

options.label: It generates heat by contracting like a muscle
options.feedback: Blubber is a passive fat layer. It does not contract, and its job is to slow heat loss, not to actively produce warmth.

options.label: It reflects the cold away from the skin
options.feedback: Cold is simply an absence of heat, not something that can be reflected. Blubber works by slowing the flow of heat, not by deflecting anything.

items.ok_line: A layer that heat crosses only very slowly, keeping the warmth from draining out.
items.ko_line: Fur works by trapping air. A whale has no fur to speak of, so the answer here has to be something else entirely.
items.exp_text: Water pulls heat away from a body far faster than air does, which leaves a swimming mammal in constant danger of losing warmth it cannot easily replace. Blubber, a thick layer of fat sitting just beneath a whale's skin, conducts heat far more slowly than muscle or blood-rich tissue would, so the warmth generated deep inside the body stays trapped rather than draining straight out into the surrounding water. Because it works through the fat itself rather than through trapped air, it keeps insulating just as well when a whale dives deep, where pressure would crush any air pocket flat.

items.prompt: How does a dolphin find prey in water too dark or murky to see through?

options.label: It sends out clicks and reads the pattern of echoes that bounce back
options.feedback: Timing and shape of the returning echoes reveal an object's distance, size and even texture, all without any need for light.

options.label: It relies on an unusually strong sense of smell underwater
options.feedback: A dolphin's sense of smell is greatly reduced, and scent does not travel through water in a way that could guide a hunt this precisely.

options.label: It detects the electric field given off by prey
options.feedback: Sensing electric fields is a talent some other animals have evolved, not dolphins, which navigate murky water a different way entirely.

options.label: It follows vibrations left behind in the prey's wake
options.feedback: A trailing wake fades quickly and reveals little about where prey is right now. Something more direct and immediate is at work here.

items.ok_line: Sound sent out, and the shape of what comes back read like a picture.
items.ko_line: This works even in complete darkness, which rules out anything that depends on light or a lingering trace left behind.
items.exp_text: A dolphin produces rapid clicks in an organ at the front of its skull, and these sounds travel outward through the water and bounce back off anything solid in their path. By timing how long each echo takes to return and comparing subtle differences picked up through its lower jaw, a dolphin builds a detailed picture of what lies ahead: its distance, its size, even whether it is a fish worth chasing. None of this depends on light at all, which is why a dolphin hunts just as effectively at night as at midday.

items.prompt: Why must a dolphin stay partly conscious even while it sleeps?

options.label: Breathing is a deliberate act it has to keep performing
options.feedback: Unlike a land mammal's automatic breathing, each breath a dolphin takes has to be a conscious choice, so it can never fully switch off.

options.label: It has to keep watch for predators at all times
options.feedback: Staying alert to danger is a real advantage of this habit, but it is not the underlying reason a dolphin cannot fully lose consciousness in the first place.

options.label: Its body temperature would drop dangerously if it fully relaxed
options.feedback: Blubber keeps a dolphin warm without any need for active muscle effort during rest. Temperature control is not what forces it to stay partly awake.

options.label: It needs to keep swimming constantly to stay afloat
options.feedback: A dolphin can rest motionless or drift without sinking. Staying afloat is not the reason it must remain partly conscious.

items.ok_line: A breath that has to be chosen, never taken for granted.
items.ko_line: In a land mammal, breathing continues automatically even during deep sleep. That is exactly what does not happen here.
items.exp_title: A breath that never becomes automatic
items.exp_text: In most mammals, breathing runs on its own, controlled unconsciously, so it continues steadily through even the deepest sleep. A dolphin's breathing never became automatic in this way; every breath is a deliberate, voluntary act, which means a fully unconscious dolphin would simply stop breathing and drown. To get the rest it needs without ever losing that control, a dolphin instead rests one half of its brain at a time, keeping the other half alert enough to surface and breathe on schedule.

items.prompt: Why does a whale's tail beat up and down, while a fish's tail sweeps side to side?

options.label: A whale's spine, inherited from land ancestors, only flexes up and down
options.feedback: A whale's ancestors walked on four legs, and a land mammal's spine bends that same way when it runs, a motion carried straight over into how the tail now swims.

options.label: A whale's tail is simply built from harder material
options.feedback: Tail material is not what decides the direction of the stroke. The direction comes from how the spine itself is able to bend.

options.label: Side-to-side movement would be too slow for a whale's size
options.feedback: Size does not force a particular direction of movement; some very large fish still swim with a side-to-side stroke. Something else decides the direction here.

options.label: A whale's tail evolved completely separately from any fish tail
options.feedback: It did evolve independently of a fish's tail, but that alone does not explain the direction it beats in. The direction traces back to an inherited skeleton.

items.ok_line: A spine built for running on land, still bending the same way it always did.
items.ko_line: Think about how a running four-legged animal's back bends with each stride, rather than about the tail on its own.
items.exp_title: A land mammal's bend, kept for swimming
items.exp_text: A whale's remote ancestors were four-legged land mammals whose spine bent up and down with each bound, the way a running dog's back arches and straightens. As that lineage moved fully into the water and its hind legs disappeared, the tail that grew in their place inherited the same up-and-down bending motion, rather than the side-to-side motion a fish's spine uses. A fish, having never been a land animal, kept the sideways bend it always had, which is why the two tails move in different directions despite doing the same job.

items.prompt: How does a seal's body cope with repeatedly plunging into cold water?

options.label: Blood flow to the skin is reduced, keeping warmth deep inside the body
options.feedback: Redirected away from the skin and toward the core and vital organs, blood loses far less heat to the cold water surrounding it.

options.label: Its heart beats faster to generate extra warmth
options.feedback: A faster heartbeat would only speed up how quickly warm blood reaches the cold skin and loses its heat. A seal's heart actually does the opposite when it dives.

options.label: Its blood vessels widen near the skin to release excess heat
options.feedback: Widening vessels near the skin would let far more heat escape into the cold water, the opposite of what keeps a diving seal warm.

options.label: It shivers continuously while swimming
options.feedback: Constant shivering would burn through energy a seal needs for the dive itself. Warmth is conserved here rather than generated by shivering.

items.ok_line: Blood pulled back from the skin, so the warmth stays where it matters most.
items.ko_line: Ask what happens to blood flow near the skin, the part of the body in direct contact with the cold.
items.exp_title: Warmth pulled inward, away from the skin
items.exp_text: As a seal enters cold water, blood vessels near its skin narrow, cutting the flow of warm blood to the surface and redirecting it toward the core of the body and the organs that need it most. With so little warm blood reaching the skin, far less heat is lost to the surrounding water, even though the skin itself grows noticeably colder in the process. Blubber beneath that skin adds a further barrier, but this redirection of blood flow is what lets a seal dive again and again without its core ever cooling down.

items.prompt: What lets a diving seal or whale hold its breath and keep functioning for so long underwater?

options.label: Its muscles store large reserves of oxygen directly
options.feedback: A protein called myoglobin, packed densely into the muscle, holds a private oxygen reserve the muscles can draw on well after the lungs are empty.

options.label: It absorbs oxygen straight from the water through its skin
options.feedback: No mammal's skin can extract oxygen dissolved in water the way a fish's gills do. Every breath still has to come from air at the surface.

options.label: Its lungs are far larger than a land mammal's of the same size
options.feedback: A diving mammal's lungs are not unusually large for its body; in fact they often collapse under pressure during a deep dive. The oxygen reserve lies elsewhere.

options.label: It slows its swimming to reduce its need for oxygen
options.feedback: A diving mammal often swims actively during a dive rather than moving as little as possible. Conserving oxygen relies on something besides simply moving less.

items.ok_line: A private store of oxygen, held inside the muscle itself.
items.ko_line: The lungs alone could not explain a dive this long. Ask where else in the body oxygen could be kept in reserve.
items.exp_title: An oxygen store built into the muscle
items.exp_text: Muscle tissue in diving mammals is packed with an oxygen-binding protein called myoglobin, present in far greater density than in a land mammal's muscle, and it holds its own private reserve of oxygen right where the muscle will need it. Alongside this, a diving mammal's heart rate drops sharply and blood flow is redirected away from organs that can briefly do without, saving the oxygen already in the blood for the muscles and brain instead. Together, these adjustments let a dive continue long after a single lungful of air would otherwise have run out.

items.prompt: How does a manatee cope with feeding on tough sea grass that wears its teeth down constantly?

options.label: Worn teeth fall out at the front and are replaced by new ones from behind
options.feedback: Continuously moving forward through the jaw, teeth arrive to replace whichever ones have worn down and dropped out ahead of them.

options.label: Its teeth are made of a mineral that cannot wear down
options.feedback: A manatee's teeth are ordinary mammal teeth, made of the same materials as any other's, and they do wear down through constant grinding.

options.label: It avoids chewing altogether and swallows sea grass whole
options.feedback: Sea grass is thoroughly chewed before being swallowed. Avoiding chewing would not solve the problem of worn teeth in the first place.

options.label: New teeth grow in only once a year
options.feedback: Replacement here runs on a continuous conveyor rather than a yearly schedule, keeping pace with wear as it happens rather than waiting for a fixed date.

items.ok_line: A conveyor of teeth, always moving forward to replace what wears away.
items.ko_line: Rather than one set of teeth for life, picture teeth constantly arriving from one direction and departing from the other.
items.exp_text: Sea grass is gritty and abrasive, and grinding through it constantly wears a manatee's molars down far faster than an ordinary mammal jaw could sustain with a single set of adult teeth. A manatee instead grows new molars continuously at the back of its jaw, and as older teeth near the front wear down to nothing, they fall out and the whole row shifts forward to take their place, much like a conveyor belt. This same replacement system evolved separately in the manatee's closest living relative, the elephant, which chews equally abrasive plant food throughout its life.

items.prompt: How does a whale calf nurse underwater without swallowing seawater along with the milk?

options.label: The mother's muscles actively squirt thick milk into the calf's mouth
options.feedback: Delivered in a rich, forceful stream by the mother's own muscle contractions, the milk is in the calf's mouth and gone before seawater has any chance to mix in.

options.label: The calf holds its breath for the entire time it is nursing
options.feedback: Holding its breath alone would not stop seawater from entering the calf's mouth alongside the milk while it tries to suckle.

options.label: The milk floats to the surface, where the calf drinks it in air
options.feedback: Whale milk is far too dense and rich to float freely, and nursing happens underwater between mother and calf, not at the surface.

options.label: The mother's teat seals directly against the calf's mouth like a hose
options.feedback: There is no such rigid seal formed between mother and calf. What actually solves the problem is the forceful way the milk itself is delivered.

items.ok_line: A rich milk fired directly into the calf's mouth, too quickly for seawater to interfere.
items.ko_line: A calf cannot suck the way a land mammal's young does underwater. Think about what the mother's body does instead.
items.exp_title: Milk delivered by force, not by suction
items.exp_text: Sucking the way a land mammal's newborn does would be difficult underwater and risk drawing in seawater along with any milk. A whale calf instead presses against its mother's body, and she actively contracts muscles around the mammary gland to squirt a thick, fat-rich stream of milk directly into its mouth. Because the milk arrives forcefully and is swallowed almost at once, there is little opportunity for seawater to mix in along the way.

items.prompt: Why does a sea otter rely on an exceptionally dense fur coat instead of a thick layer of blubber like a whale or seal?

options.label: Its small body cannot hold enough blubber to insulate well
options.feedback: A body as small as an otter's loses heat to the water too quickly for a fat layer alone to keep up, so it depends on trapped air in fur instead.

options.label: Blubber would make an otter too heavy to float
options.feedback: A layer of fat, being less dense than water, would help an otter float rather than sink. Weight is not the reason it relies on fur instead.

options.label: Fur is more effective than blubber against any predator
options.feedback: Fur offers essentially no defence against a predator. Its value to an otter lies entirely in keeping the animal warm, not in protection.

options.label: An otter cannot digest the fat needed to build blubber
options.feedback: An otter has no trouble digesting fat in its diet. What limits it is the small size of its body, not any difficulty digesting fat.

items.ok_line: A body too small for blubber to keep up, so fur carries the job instead.
items.ko_line: Think about how quickly a small body loses heat to cold water compared with a much larger one.
items.exp_title: Too small for blubber to keep pace
items.exp_text: A small body loses heat to cold water far faster relative to its size than a large one does, which leaves little time for a modest layer of blubber to hold that heat in. A sea otter instead grows the densest fur of any mammal, so thick that a layer of trapped air sits permanently against its skin and keeps water from ever touching it directly. Keeping that layer intact takes constant grooming, since matted or oiled fur lets water reach the skin and strips the insulation away almost immediately.
